Relativists critique universalist interventions for hypocrisy, noting Western tolerance of analogous body modifications—like male circumcision, performed on over a million U.S. infants annually without equivalent condemnation, or elective cosmetic surgeries such as labiaplasty—while selectively targeting non-Western traditions, thereby revealing culturally biased standards rather than consistent ethical principles.

In contrast, universal human rights advocates maintain that FGM constitutes a fundamental violation of bodily autonomy and dignity, transcending cultural boundaries, as affirmed by international frameworks Sudan has engaged with, including its 2006 ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), which prohibits practices discriminating against women. [61]

These proponents assert that empirical patterns of coercion—evident in Sudanese communities where girls face familial pressure irrespective of personal consent—justify overriding relativist deference to sovereignty, prioritizing protections akin to those against child labor or forced marriage, with UN bodies like UNICEF framing FGM as incompatible with the universal right to physical integrity under the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Sudanese-specific inquiries reveal tensions in this debate, with qualitative studies indicating that human rights-based campaigns are frequently perceived as neocolonial impositions, alienating potential allies and reinforcing FGM as a marker of cultural resistance; for instance, ethnographic work documents how urban and rural respondents in Sudan view top-down legal bans as eroding local agency, leading to clandestine practices rather than abandonment. [7]

This perception persists despite declining support for severe forms, as evidenced by community-level shifts toward less invasive variants, suggesting that relativist sensitivities to sovereignty may facilitate gradual change more effectively than absolutist mandates, though universalists counter that delays perpetuate non-consensual harms without accountability.
Critiques of anti-FGM strategies in Sudan center on their limited empirical impact, with legal bans failing to substantially reduce prevalence despite widespread implementation.

The 2020 national criminalization, punishable by up to three years imprisonment, has correlated with evasion rather than elimination, as families relocate girls to rural areas or states with laxer enforcement during school closures or holidays, exploiting enforcement gaps amid the COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing instability. [63]

Reports indicate no verified post-ban surveys showing more than marginal declines—prevalence hovered around 87% for women aged 15-49 prior to the ban, with anecdotal evidence of sustained or even increased cases in urban centers like Khartoum due to secrecy and medicalization by midwives. [1]

This ineffectiveness stems from a reliance on coercive measures that ignore underlying causal drivers, such as economic incentives for practitioners (e.g., midwives earning supplemental income from cuttings amid low base salaries of $75-128 monthly) and social pressures prioritizing conformity over penalties. [25]

Prior attempts at criminalization, including state-level bans in Darfur and Gedaref since the 2000s, similarly yielded evasion and cultural backlash, framing prohibitions as Western impositions that galvanized conservative resistance without altering entrenched norms. [22]

International NGOs and media, often institutionally inclined toward highlighting legislative "wins" to sustain funding and narratives, have overstated progress—e.g., touting the 2020 ban as transformative—while downplaying persistent high rates and enforcement voids, potentially reflecting biases that prioritize symbolic victories over rigorous outcome tracking.
In contrast, non-coercive pilots emphasizing aligned incentives demonstrate greater promise.

A 2016-2018 health sector intervention trained 31% of community midwives on FGM harms, securing voluntary pledges to abandon the practice from the same proportion without punitive threats, shifting intent among key performers who conduct 64% of cases. [25]

Such approaches, integrating education with accountability frameworks and indirect economic support via donor-funded trainings, avoid resistance by addressing practitioners' motivations, outperforming bans that drive underground activity; scaling similar incentive-based models, potentially including subsidies for alternative livelihoods, could yield more sustainable reductions than prohibition alone.

The persistence of female genital mutilation (FGM) in Sudan entrenches gender imbalances by embedding cultural norms that tie women's social value to perceived chastity and family honor, often resulting in stigma, harassment, and reduced marriage prospects for uncircumcised girls, thereby limiting female autonomy and perpetuating intergenerational cycles of control by elder women. [2] [6]

This sustains broader societal disparities, as affected women face chronic health complications—including urogenital disorders, obstetric risks during childbirth, and psychological trauma—that impair productivity and impose ongoing burdens on limited healthcare resources. [64]

Rapid or mandate-driven abolition efforts carry risks of social disruption in tightly knit communities, where non-compliance invites familial pressure, exclusion, or even unauthorized procedures by relatives, potentially shifting practices underground or toward less severe forms without addressing underlying stigma. [2]

Prior state-level bans, such as those in Khartoum and Gadarif, have demonstrated limited efficacy and increased secrecy rather than cessation, highlighting how coercive approaches may exacerbate resistance without viable cultural alternatives.

Evidence indicates a slow, organic decline in FGM prevalence linked to urbanization and education, with urban rates at 85.5% compared to 87.2% in rural areas, and support for continuation dropping below 24% in Khartoum versus a national average of 41%, driven by greater access to awareness campaigns and professional opportunities. [66] [2]

However, the civil war since April 2023 has reversed such gains by destroying up to 80% of health facilities, displacing millions, and heightening poverty-driven vulnerabilities, likely postponing meaningful eradication by decades as anti-FGM initiatives falter amid service collapses and rising gender-based violence.

Female genital mutilation (FGM) in the Gambia is a customary practice entailing the partial or total excision of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical purposes, most often conducted on girls before age five by traditional circumcisers using rudimentary tools. [1]

The procedure, prevalent across ethnic groups including Mandinka, Fula, and Wolof, and irrespective of Muslim or Christian affiliation, serves purported social cohesion functions such as controlling female sexuality and marking rites of passage, with 72.6% of women aged 15–49 affected according to the 2019–20 Demographic and Health Survey, down marginally from 74.9% in 2013. [1]

Enacted via the 2015 Women's (Amendment) Act, Gambian law criminalizes performing, aiding, or abetting FGM with penalties up to three years imprisonment or fines equivalent to $1,250, aligning with international obligations under treaties like the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. [3] [2]
Enforcement has been minimal, with only two prosecutions prior to the first convictions in 2023 for cutting infants, underscoring weak implementation amid cultural entrenchment. [3]

In 2024, a parliamentary bill to repeal the ban advanced initially but was rejected following domestic activism and external advocacy, preserving the prohibition despite claims by some religious figures that it conflicts with tradition. [2]

Predominantly Type I (clitoridectomy) or Type II (excision), with 16.6% involving infibulation (Type III), the practice correlates with elevated health risks including hemorrhage, urinary issues, and obstetric complications—studies indicate 77% of adverse neonatal outcomes link to FGM-affected mothers—compounded by a reported 34.3% lifetime health problems among cut women. [2] [1]

Support for continuation has waned to 45.7% among women 15–49, particularly with rising education and wealth, fueling UNFPA-UNICEF initiatives like mothers' clubs reaching thousands via dialogues and alternative rites to shift norms. [2] [4]

Cross-border practices with Senegal persist, but regional pacts and data systems aim to bolster monitoring, though abandonment hinges on addressing underlying social networks enforcing conformity. [4]

Female genital mutilation (FGM) in The Gambia traces its origins to ancient practices predating Islam and Christianity, with anthropological evidence suggesting roots extending over 2,000 years, possibly linked to early customs in regions like 5th-century BC Egypt or among Equatorial African herders for protective or sacrificial purposes. [5]

In Gambian context, it emerged as a self-enforcing social convention upheld by community expectations across ethnic groups, transmitted generationally through families and elders, independent of religious mandates despite later associations with Islam by some adherents. [5]

The practice holds profound traditional significance as a rite of passage marking the transition to womanhood, particularly among groups like the Mandinka, where it forms part of the nyaakaa initiation ritual performed between ages four and ten, transforming uninitiated girls (solima) into socially mature individuals prepared for marriage and motherhood. [5]

During multi-week seclusion periods, initiates learn values such as respect, obedience, endurance, and secrecy—concepts encapsulated as "knowing the eye"—alongside practical skills, songs, and proverbs, reinforcing subservience and community roles. [5]

It is justified culturally to ensure virginity, prevent promiscuity, control female sexuality, enhance cleanliness and aesthetic beauty, and uphold family honor, with uncut girls facing stigma as immature or unclean, often barring them from social ceremonies. [6] [7]
Among the Sarahule, it occurs in infancy without elaborate ceremony but is viewed as essential for purity; Fula subgroups similarly emphasize sealing to guarantee fidelity.

Prevalence and significance vary ethnically, with near-universal adoption among Mandinka (96.7%), Sarahule (97.8%), Fula (87.3%), and Jola/Karoninka (87%), where it signals ethnic identity and social integration, contrasted by low rates among Wolof (12.4%) and Serer (43-46%). [6] [5]

These beliefs prioritize marriageability and communal acceptance, with grandmothers often deciding based on norms that equate FGM with a girl's status and her family's reputation, perpetuated by elder women circumcisers who derive authority from the tradition. [5]
In The Gambia, female genital mutilation (FGM) primarily consists of procedures classified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as Type I and Type II, with Type I being the most common. [6] [8]
Type I, or clitoridectomy, involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or its prepuce. [6]
In a 2013 clinical examination of 570 Gambian women aged 15-49, Type I accounted for 57.2% of cases among those who had undergone FGM. [6]
Type II, or excision, entails the partial or total removal of the clitoris and labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora; this type represented 18.4% of cases in the same study.
These procedures are traditionally carried out by elderly female excisers, known as traditional practitioners, who perform 97% of cuttings on girls and women aged 15-49. [8]

The cutting occurs without anesthesia or sterile conditions, using rudimentary sharp instruments such as knives or razors, often leading to imprecise excision that may extend beyond the targeted tissues. [6]

Girls typically undergo the procedure between birth and preadolescence, before menarche or marriage; among women aged 15-49, 55% were cut before age five, 28% between ages five and nine, and 7% between ages ten and 14. [8]
Type III (infibulation), involving narrowing of the vaginal opening through apposition of the labia, is rare, observed in only 0.4% of the examined sample. [6]
Type IV procedures, such as pricking or scraping, have been reported anecdotally but lack quantified prevalence in Gambian data.

Variations in procedure extent occur across ethnic groups practicing FGM extensively, including Mandinka, Fula, Sarahule, and Jola, where prevalence within these groups exceeds 94% for women aged 15-49; these groups favor Types I and II without routine infibulation. [6]
Post-procedure, wounds are sometimes bound or treated with herbal pastes to promote healing and adhesion, though medical intervention is absent in traditional settings.
According to the 2019-20 Gambia Demographic and Health Survey (GDHS), 73% of women aged 15-49 have undergone female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C). [10]
This national prevalence reflects data from a representative sample of over 11,000 women, capturing self-reported experiences of the procedure. [10]
Among girls aged 0-14, 46% had been subjected to FGM/C at the time of the survey, with higher rates (60%) among daughters of circumcised mothers.
