These disparities align with population density and access to awareness campaigns, though enforcement of the 2015 ban remains inconsistent across regions. [10]
Earlier surveys, such as the 2013 DHS, reported a slightly higher national figure of 75%, indicating a modest decline over time.

In The Gambia, female genital mutilation (FGM) prevalence varies significantly by ethnic group, with the practice deeply embedded in the traditions of certain communities while largely absent in others.

Among the major ethnic groups, Sarahuleh exhibit the highest rates, with 76% of girls undergoing FGM, followed by Mandinka/Jahanka at 54%, Bambara at 50%, Fula/Tukulor/Lorobo at 46%, and Jola/Karoninka at 43%. [11]
In contrast, groups such as Wollof, Creole/Aku (19%), Serere (9%), and Manjago (4%) show much lower or negligible prevalence, reflecting cultural norms that do not incorporate the practice. [11] [9]

Overall, for women aged 15-49, ethnic variations range from as low as 14% to as high as 95%, underscoring how FGM serves as a marker of group identity in practicing communities like Mandinka, Jola, Sarahule, and Fula, but is rejected by non-practicing ones such as Wolof and Serere. [7]
[Table]
Social factors further modulate these ethnic patterns.

Education level inversely correlates with the practice: among mothers of girls aged 0-14, 77% of those with no education report their daughters cut, versus 72% with primary and 68% with secondary or higher education, indicating that formal schooling disrupts transmission by challenging cultural justifications. [7]

Wealth shows less consistent patterns, with middle-quintile households at 47% for girls, higher than the poorest (39%) or richest (34%), suggesting that socioeconomic status alone does not drive abandonment but interacts with ethnic and geographic influences. [11]
Support for continuation also varies ethnically, from 68% in high-prevalence groups to 10% in low-prevalence ones among informed women aged 15-49.

Physical effects of female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in The Gambia include immediate complications such as hemorrhage, acute anemia, and infections like tetanus, cystitis, and septicaemia, reported in 12.6% of cases seeking prompt medical attention after the procedure. [12]

Long-term physical consequences encompass chronic gynecological issues, with women subjected to type I FGM/C (clitoridectomy, comprising 66.2% of cases) experiencing dysmenorrhea in 58.2% of instances, recurrent urinary tract infections in 19.6%, and painful intercourse in 29.3%, while type II (excision, 26.3% of cases) shows elevated rates of 67.6%, 44.2%, and 57.1%, respectively, compared to 34.5%, 14.4%, and 12.9% in uncut women (all p < 0.001). [6] [12]

Anomalous healing manifests as fibrosis (15.8–19.4%), keloid formation (13.3–35.6% on clitoris, up to 21.6% on labia), synechia (7.1–54.4%), and clitoral neuroma (8.1–20.6%), absent in uncut controls.

Obstetric complications are markedly increased, with 39.0% of type I and 65.9% of type II cases facing delivery issues like perineal tears (27.8–48.8%), prolonged labor (15.6–36.6%), and episiotomy needs (20.0–30.5%), yielding odds ratios of 4.82–9.06 relative to uncut women (11.7% complications); fresh stillbirths occur in 2.9–6.1% of affected deliveries versus 0%. [6]
Newborns of cut mothers experience higher rates of fetal distress (8.8–26.8%) and caput succedaneum (14.6–34.2%), with overall complications in 15.6–37.8% versus 5.3% (odds ratio 5.17). [6]
Overall, 34.3% of Gambian women examined for FGM/C-related issues report either immediate or delayed physical effects, including persistent scarring and dyspareunia across all types.

Psychological effects in Gambian girls post-FGC include probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) at 19.2% prevalence among 12-year-olds, though only 4.2% attribute it directly to FGC, with 95.8% linked to confounding serious life events like violence or bereavement (average 4.5 events per girl). [13]

Girls citing FGC as most bothersome (16.8%) show lower PTSD rates (4.8%) and better functioning than those affected by other traumas (22.1%), indicating FGC's trauma may be overshadowed by broader adversities; physical complications like genital pain do not significantly correlate with PTSD attribution in this cohort. [13]

General literature on FGM/C notes associations with anxiety, depression, and sexual dysfunction, potentially exacerbated by physical sequelae, but Gambia-specific data emphasize multifactorial mental health burdens rather than isolated FGC causation.

In The Gambia, female genital mutilation (FGM), locally termed "female circumcision," is often justified as a rite of passage marking a girl's transition to womanhood and social maturity, particularly among ethnic groups like the Mandinka, where it forms part of the nyaakaa initiation ritual for girls aged four to ten.

This process, involving seclusion and instruction from elder women, is believed to instill essential virtues such as respect (horomo), secrecy (suturo), and endurance (sabati), collectively known as "knowing the eye," preparing girls for roles in marriage and motherhood while reinforcing community values of obedience and discretion. [15]

Proponents argue that the pain endured during the procedure teaches resilience and discipline, with respondents in qualitative studies describing it as a "school" for proper behavior among elders, thereby enhancing a girl's social standing and eligibility for inclusion in communal events.

Local beliefs emphasize FGM's role in controlling female sexuality to preserve purity and prevent promiscuity, with many Gambians asserting that uncut girls "like men too much" or risk premarital sex, pregnancy, or infidelity, thus safeguarding family honor and marital fidelity. [16]

It is perceived to reduce excessive sexual desire, making women less demanding in marriage and averting risks like divorce or prostitution, while also ensuring physical "sealing" of virginity until wedlock in practices akin to Type III FGM among groups like the Sarahule and some Fula. [15]

Hygiene and aesthetic ideals further underpin justifications, as the procedure is said to eliminate "bad smells," prevent abnormal clitoral growth, and promote cleanliness aligned with Islamic purity norms, rendering uncut women (solima in Mandinka) impure, disrespectful, or unfit for prayer and social interactions. [16]

Social conformity drives adherence, with uncircumcised individuals facing stigma, ostracism, or exclusion from ceremonies, compelling families to comply to maintain ethnic and communal acceptance, especially in rural areas where prevalence exceeds 90% among Mandinka (96.7%) and Sarahule (97.8%) women aged 15-49. [15]

Religious rationales, though not explicitly mandated by the Quran, draw on select hadiths referencing "female circumcision" as a virtuous Islamic practice (sunna), with leaders like Imam Abdoulie Fatty and the Gambia Supreme Islamic Council framing it as essential for piety and cultural preservation against external impositions. [18]

Defenders, including lawmakers and practitioners, equate it to male circumcision and argue that bans infringe on constitutional rights to religious and ethnic traditions, viewing abandonment as a threat to societal norms upheld across generations. [17]

Among ethnic minorities like the Wolof, where prevalence is lower (12.4%), justifications weaken, but in dominant groups, the practice sustains intergenerational transmission, with elders overriding individual choice to preserve group identity and economic roles for cutters. [15]
These perceptions persist despite health risks, as cultural continuity is prioritized, with surveys indicating over 70% support in regions like Brikama and Mansakonko.

Prior to the enactment of specific legislation in 2015, female genital mutilation (FGM) in The Gambia lacked any dedicated legal prohibition under national law, despite its widespread practice across ethnic groups and regions. [19]

The practice persisted without criminalization during the colonial period under British rule and in the post-independence era following 1965, reflecting its entrenched cultural status rather than formal legal endorsement or restriction.
In December 2015, the Gambian government passed the Women's (Amendment) Act 2015, amending the 2010 Women's Act to explicitly criminalize FGM. [19]

Sections 32A and 32B of the amended act define FGM as the partial or total removal of external female genitalia or other injury to female genital organs for non-therapeutic reasons, imposing penalties of a fine of up to 50,000 Dalasi, imprisonment for a term of up to three years, or both, with life imprisonment if the procedure causes death. [21]

This legislation marked the first national ban, prompted by President Yahya Jammeh's public declaration in November 2015 that FGM was "un-Islamic" and would no longer be tolerated, framing the prohibition in religious terms to align with the country's predominantly Muslim population.

The 2015 act represented a shift from prior inaction, influenced by international pressure from organizations like UNICEF and the African Union, though enforcement remained limited in its initial years due to cultural resistance and weak institutional capacity. [22]
No earlier Gambian statutes, such as those on child protection or general assault, were systematically applied to FGM cases prior to this amendment, allowing the practice to continue unchecked.

The Women's (Amendment) Act 2015 criminalizes performing female genital mutilation (FGM) under Section 32A(1), with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of 50,000 Dalasi (approximately US$1,060), or both; if the procedure causes death, the punishment is life imprisonment. [21]

Section 32B(1) imposes the same penalties on those who request, incite, or promote FGM by providing tools or other means, while failure to report known or impending FGM without good cause incurs a fine of 10,000 Dalasi (approximately US$212). [21]

These provisions apply universally, including to traditional circumcisers, parents, and accomplices, supported by complementary laws such as the Children's Act 2005 and Criminal Code 1933, which address harm to children and grievous bodily injury.

Enforcement relies on coordination among the Ministries of Women's Affairs, Justice, Health, and Social Welfare, alongside the National Steering Committee on FGM and community surveillance systems established with NGO support, such as GAMCOTRAP and UNFPA initiatives since 2021. [23] [21]
Prosecutions remain rare; as of 2024, convictions have been secured only in the landmark 2023 case.

In August 2023, the Kaur/Kuntaur Magistrates Court convicted three women for performing FGM on three infants (aged 4 months to 1 year) in Bakadagi-Mandinka village, fining each 15,000 Dalasi with a one-year prison alternative, following intervention that prevented the procedure on five other girls. [23] [24]
An earlier 2016 case involving a child's death from FGM yielded no reported follow-through, highlighting inconsistent judicial follow-up.

Compliance is undermined by persistent cultural entrenchment, with approximately 76% of women aged 15–49 having undergone FGM, often before age six, and widespread community resistance viewing the practice as a religious or traditional rite. [24]

The procedure continues clandestinely, particularly in rural areas and across borders with high-prevalence neighbors like Senegal, evading detection due to underreporting and assurances from influential figures that perpetrators face no repercussions. [24] [21]

A 2024 private bill to repeal the ban, rejected by the National Assembly in July after public debate, exposed ongoing pushback, with proponents citing cultural accommodations despite the law's preservation signaling nominal political commitment. [24]

Gaps include inadequate training for law enforcers, limited victim protections, and absence of explicit provisions against medicalized or extraterritorial FGM, contributing to weak deterrence and sustained non-compliance.
Anti-FGM campaigns in The Gambia have intensified since the 2015 enactment of the Women's (Amendment) Act, which criminalized the practice with penalties of up to three years imprisonment and fines.

Local organizations, including women's networks and religious leaders, have spearheaded community-based initiatives, such as advocacy through imams' sermons to challenge cultural and religious justifications for FGM.

For instance, in rural areas, illiterate women like Amie Jatta Njie have mobilized peers via door-to-door education and village meetings to promote alternatives to the tradition, emphasizing health risks and legal consequences.
These grassroots efforts often collaborate with national bodies like the Ministry of Women's Affairs, focusing on awareness in high-prevalence ethnic groups such as the Mandinka and Fula.
International organizations have provided substantial support, funding, and technical assistance to bolster these campaigns.

The UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation, operational in The Gambia since 2008, has trained over 1,000 community influencers, including traditional cutters who renounce the practice, and supported public declarations against FGM in 15% of targeted villages by 2023.

UNICEF has also engaged youth advocates, such as Nafisa Binte Jobe, who testified in parliament against repeal efforts, while UNFPA facilitated cross-border dialogues with Senegal and Guinea to curb FGM migration.

In 2024, amid threats to repeal the ban, global entities like the World Health Organization and UN Women issued statements reinforcing The Gambia's commitments under the Maputo Protocol and Sustainable Development Goal 5.3, which aims to eliminate harmful practices by 2030. [26] [27]

A pivotal campaign victory occurred on July 15, 2024, when parliament rejected a bill to decriminalize FGM, following intense lobbying by activists like Jaha Dukureh of Safe Hands for Girls, who credited international pressure from UN agencies and NGOs such as Amnesty International for swaying votes.
This outcome preserved the ban amid religious opposition, with UN officials hailing it as a "monumental achievement" aligned with human rights treaties.

However, Amnesty noted persistent root causes, urging sustained investment in education and economic alternatives for cutters, as campaigns have contributed to a slight decline in prevalence from 74.9% in 2013 to 72.6% in 2019–20 according to the Demographic and Health Survey, though enforcement remains uneven. [29] [30] [3] [1]

International donors, including the European Union and U.S. Agency for International Development, have channeled over $5 million annually into prevention since 2015, prioritizing survivor-led advocacy to counter cultural resistance.

Proponents of female genital mutilation (FGM) in The Gambia defend the practice as an integral component of cultural identity and social cohesion, viewing it as a rite of passage that marks a girl's transition to womanhood and ensures her eligibility for marriage within ethnic communities such as the Mandinka, Fula, and Jola. [18]

Local beliefs hold that FGM preserves virginity, curbs promiscuity, and maintains family honor by controlling female sexuality, with uncut women often stigmatized as impure or capable of contaminating food, rendering it haram under traditional interpretations. [18]

Cutters, typically respected elderly women, derive social status from performing the procedure, which is passed down generationally and reinforces community bonds, as evidenced by statements from practitioners who refuse to abandon it despite incentives.

Religious justifications form a core defense, with many Gambians, including 53% of women surveyed in 2019-2020, believing FGM fulfills an Islamic obligation derived from certain hadiths, despite its absence from the Quran and pre-Islamic origins. [17]

The Gambia Supreme Islamic Council issued a fatwa in September 2023 declaring female circumcision a "virtue of Islam," urging reconsideration of the 2015 ban, while Imam Abdoulie Fatty has campaigned to "restore" it, equating opposition to an assault on Islam and paying fines for convicted cutters in 2023. [18]

Proponents like National Assembly Member Sulayman Saho distinguish it from mutilation, advocating only the removal of the clitoral tip—analogous to male circumcision—while questioning the relevance of global data to Gambian contexts.

Cultural resistance manifests in political and communal pushback against the ban, including a 2024 Women's (Amendment) Bill introduced by MP Almameh Gibba to repeal it, which passed second reading with 43 of 47 votes before stalling amid international scrutiny. [31]

Supporters frame the law as a Western imposition eroding sovereignty, with protests chanting "Gambia is not for sale" and decrying it as colonial interference, leading to legal challenges citing constitutional rights to religious and cultural freedoms under Sections 25 and 32. [31]

Despite the ban's affirmation in July 2024, underground continuation persists, driven by fears that abandonment would dishonor ancestors and disrupt social norms, as articulated by community elders who prioritize tradition over external health critiques.

In December 2015, President Yahya Jammeh signed the Women's (Amendment) Act, criminalizing female genital mutilation (FGM) with penalties of up to three years imprisonment and fines, marking the first national ban on the practice in The Gambia where prevalence exceeded 75% among women. [32]

The legislation targeted all forms of FGM, including on minors and adults, amid international pressure and local advocacy, though enforcement remained limited in subsequent years due to cultural entrenchment.

In 2016, The Gambia's parliament adopted the National Strategic and Action Plan for the Promotion of the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (2016-2020), outlining community sensitization, legal enforcement, and survivor support to reduce prevalence from an estimated 76.3% in adult women. [34]

This followed a 2013 Demographic and Health Survey confirming high rates across ethnic groups, with the plan emphasizing partnerships with NGOs and religious leaders despite resistance from traditional cutters and communities viewing FGM as a rite of passage.

From 2017 to 2022, no major prosecutions occurred under the ban, with surveys indicating persistent practice rates around 70-75%, often conducted clandestinely on infants to evade scrutiny, as reported by anti-FGM organizations tracking underground operations. [35]
International funding supported awareness campaigns, but local compliance lagged, with cut cases rarely reported due to community complicity and fear of reprisal.

In August 2023, authorities filed the first criminal charges for FGM since the ban, indicting three women in connection with performing the procedure, highlighting emerging enforcement efforts amid rising advocacy pressures.

In March 2024, National Assembly Member Fatoumata Ceesay-Jallow introduced a private member's bill to repeal sections of the 2015 Act banning FGM, arguing it violated cultural and religious norms; the assembly voted 31-4 to advance it for debate despite committee recommendations against. [37]

This sparked international condemnation from UNICEF, UNFPA, and Human Rights Watch, who cited risks to girls' health and rights, with prevalence data showing over 70% of women aged 15-49 still affected. [38]

On July 15, 2024, The Gambia's National Assembly voted 31-18 to reject the repeal bill, upholding the 2015 ban following intense lobbying by activists like Jaha Dukureh and global bodies including the UN, which hailed it as a "monumental achievement" for protecting over 200,000 girls at risk annually. [30] [29]
The decision underscored tensions between cultural preservation and human rights, with Amnesty International urging stronger root-cause interventions like education to sustain progress.
Enforcement of Gambia's 2015 ban on female genital mutilation (FGM) remains inconsistent, with reports indicating limited prosecutions and widespread non-compliance in rural areas.

As of 2023, only a handful of cases have reached the courts since the law's enactment, including landmark convictions in August 2023 where three women were found guilty and fined D15,000 (or one year imprisonment in default) for performing FGM on infants, marking the first such convictions under the ban. [23]

Despite this, human rights organizations note that enforcement is hampered by cultural entrenchment, lack of political will, and inadequate resources for monitoring, with a prevalence of 72.6% among women aged 15–49 as of the 2019–20 Demographic and Health Survey, reflecting high ongoing risk to girls.

Challenges to ongoing enforcement include resistance from religious and community leaders who frame FGM as an Islamic obligation, despite scholarly rebuttals from Gambian imams in 2023 fatwas declaring it un-Islamic.

Government initiatives, such as the National Action Plan Against FGM (2021-2025), aim to bolster community education and survivor support, but implementation is uneven, with funding shortfalls reported by NGOs in 2024.
International partners like UNICEF and the EU have provided training for law enforcement, yet corruption and underreporting persist, as village-level excisions often evade detection.
Future prospects for eradication appear guarded, contingent on sustained advocacy and economic incentives to shift norms.

Projections from 2023 studies suggest that without intensified enforcement, prevalence could decline only modestly to 60% by 2030, driven by urbanization and youth-led campaigns rather than legal measures alone.

Optimistic scenarios hinge on expanding alternative rites of passage programs, which have shown success in select communities by preserving cultural elements without cutting, potentially accelerating abandonment if scaled nationally.
However, political shifts, including potential Islamist influences, could undermine progress, as evidenced by a 2022 parliamentary push to repeal the ban that was narrowly defeated.

Female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United Kingdom encompasses procedures that intentionally alter or injure the female genital organs for cultural or other non-therapeutic reasons, a practice imported primarily through migration from high-prevalence countries in sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, such as Somalia (98% national prevalence), Sudan (87%), and Egypt (87%). [1]

Despite being criminalized under the Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act 1985 and expanded by the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003—as amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015, which imposes penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment and extends extraterritorial jurisdiction—FGM continues within affected diaspora communities, with estimates of around 137,000 women and girls born in practising countries residing in England and Wales in 2011, approximately 103,000 of them aged 15–49 having undergone the procedure. [2] [3]

Prevalence is concentrated in urban areas like London (21 per 1,000 population) and cities including Manchester and Birmingham, reflecting patterns of settlement from origin countries where FGM rates exceed 65–98% among women aged 15–49. [3]

An additional 10,000 girls aged 0–14 in England and Wales were estimated at risk in 2011, with UK-wide figures suggesting up to 60,000 girls under 15 potentially vulnerable, often during "cutting seasons" involving travel abroad. [3]

Enforcement has proven challenging, with mandatory reporting duties for health and social care professionals since 2015 yielding thousands of NHS records of affected individuals—yet the first conviction for FGM occurred only in 2019, despite laws in place for over 30 years, followed by sparse subsequent cases including a 2024 conspiracy conviction. [2] [4] [5]

Prosecutorial hurdles include evidentiary requirements for proving mutilation, victim reluctance due to familial pressures, and jurisdictional complexities for overseas acts, resulting in a stark disparity between identified prevalence and judicial outcomes. [2]

This under-prosecution, amid health data revealing persistent complications like childbirth risks for affected women (comprising 1.5% of annual deliveries in England and Wales), underscores debates over cultural persistence versus legal deterrence in multicultural settings. [3]
Efforts include FGM protection orders and public awareness campaigns, though empirical gaps in post-migration attitude shifts limit precise risk assessments for UK-born girls. [2]

In United Kingdom law, female genital mutilation (FGM) is defined under Section 1 of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 as the excision, infibulation, or other mutilation of the whole or any part of a girl's labia majora, labia minora, or clitoris. [6]

"Excise" refers to cutting out, removing, or extracting genital tissue; "infibulate" involves closing off or obstructing the genitalia, including suturing or re-infibulation; and "mutilate" encompasses severe wounding, disfigurement, or deprivation of organ function, which need not be permanent and may include procedures temporarily altering appearance. [2]

These acts constitute offences regardless of consent or location if involving UK nationals or residents, with limited exemptions for necessary medical procedures performed by registered practitioners. [6]

UK authorities, including the Crown Prosecution Service and National Health Service, recognize the World Health Organization's classification of FGM into four types, though the legal definition is not strictly limited to these and extends to any non-therapeutic harmful procedures under the "otherwise mutilates" provision. [2]
[Table]
- Type 1 (clitoridectomy): Partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or its prepuce.
- Type 2 (excision): Partial or total removal of the clitoris and labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora.

- Type 3 (infibulation): Narrowing of the vaginal opening through cutting and repositioning the inner or outer labia, often with removal of the clitoris, creating a seal that may require surgical reopening for intercourse or childbirth.

- Type 4: All other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical reasons, including pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, or cauterizing, which may qualify as mutilation depending on the risk and injury caused. [7]
These types encompass procedures performed with or without anaesthesia, often using rudimentary tools, and are prosecuted as child abuse when involving girls under 18.

The Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act 1985 was the first UK legislation specifically criminalizing female genital mutilation (FGM), making it an offence to excise, infibulate or otherwise mutilate the whole or any part of the labia majora, labia minora or clitoris of another person, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment.

This Act applied to acts performed in the UK but did not extraterritorially cover UK nationals or residents committing FGM abroad, nor did it address related preparatory acts or extra-familial cutting.
While the primary legislation described applies to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have equivalent statutes with similar prohibitions and penalties.

The Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 replaced the 1985 law, extending extraterritorial jurisdiction to UK nationals or permanent residents for FGM performed abroad, with a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment and/or a fine.
It also criminalized assisting a girl to undergo FGM, including arrangements for travel, but enforcement remained limited due to evidential challenges and cultural sensitivities.

Further amendments came via the Serious Crime Act 2015, which introduced FGM Protection Orders (FGMPOs) to safeguard at-risk girls through civil measures like prohibiting travel or contact, with breaches punishable by up to five years' imprisonment; it also raised the criminal penalty for FGM to life imprisonment if the victim is under the age of 16, and added offences for failing to protect a girl from FGM.

The 2015 Act mandated reporting by regulated health and social care professionals of known FGM cases in under-18s to authorities, aiming to improve detection, though compliance data from NHS sources indicate under-reporting persists.

Prosecutions under these laws carry additional penalties for related offences, such as conspiracy or aiding under general criminal law, with courts able to impose Sexual Harm Prevention Orders alongside FGM convictions; for instance, the first successful prosecution in 2019 resulted in 11 years' imprisonment for a mother convicted under the 2003 Act.
Despite these frameworks, conviction rates remain low, with only a handful of cases since 1985, attributed by official reviews to evidential difficulties rather than legislative inadequacy.

In England and Wales, a 2015 study using 2011 Census data estimated that 103,229 women aged 15–49 born in countries where female genital mutilation (FGM) is concentrated had likely undergone the procedure, based on applying country-specific prevalence rates from Demographic and Health Surveys and Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys to migrant populations. [9]

This figure excludes girls under 15 and those born in the UK to parents from high-prevalence countries, with additional estimates suggesting around 24,000 girls aged 0-14 born in such countries resided there at the time, some of whom may have already undergone or were at risk of FGM. [9]

These extrapolations provide the primary national prevalence benchmark, though they rely on assumptions about uniform application of origin-country rates to diaspora groups and do not account for post-2011 migration or variations in practice among immigrants.

The NHS FGM Enhanced Dataset, implemented mandatorily in England from April 2015, tracks healthcare attendances where FGM is identified or confirmed, offering insight into known cases but underrepresenting total prevalence due to non-attendance, unreported procedures, and incomplete recording. [10]
From April 2015 to March 2024, 37,615 individual women and girls were recorded across 102,155 attendances at NHS hospitals and GP practices in England. [10]
For the most recent full year (April 2023 to March 2024), there were 14,355 such attendances. [10]

Data indicate that Type 3 FGM (infibulation) accounts for a plurality of recorded cases, with most procedures occurring before age 1 or between ages 1-4, and primary countries of birth including Somalia, Egypt, and Sudan.
Regional variations show concentrations in areas with higher immigration from FGM-practicing countries, per the 2015 prevalence estimates.
London boroughs hosted the largest numbers, with Brent estimated at over 3,000 affected women aged 15+, followed by Newham, Ealing, and Tower Hamlets each exceeding 2,000. [9]
Outside London, high estimates included Leicester (around 1,500), Birmingham, and Manchester local authorities. [9]

NHS attendance data for 2023-2024 corroborate urban clustering, with breakdowns available by integrated care boards and local authorities revealing elevated rates in London and the West Midlands, though exact regional totals are not aggregated nationally in summaries. [10]

Comparable systematic data for Scotland and Northern Ireland remain limited, with scoping studies indicating far lower prevalence tied to smaller at-risk migrant populations, and no equivalent mandatory health datasets.

Police-recorded FGM offences remain sparse, reflecting underreporting and prosecutorial challenges rather than incidence; honour-based abuse statistics, which encompass FGM, recorded 18,000 incidents in England and Wales for the year ending March 2024, but specific FGM offences numbered fewer than 100 annually in recent years, with no breakdown by region in public releases.

Female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United Kingdom primarily affects immigrant communities originating from countries in Africa where the practice is culturally entrenched, with the highest concentrations among those from the Horn of Africa and parts of North and West Africa.

According to estimates from 2011 census data and national surveys, approximately 137,000 women and girls born in FGM-practicing countries were living in England and Wales with the procedure, representing about 4.8 per 1,000 of the female population. [3]
Of these, over half of the women aged 15–49 (around 53,000) originated from Horn of Africa nations where FGM prevalence exceeds 90% and Type III infibulation is common.

The Somali community constitutes one of the largest affected groups, with national FGM prevalence in Somalia at 98% among women aged 15–49, leading to significant numbers of Somali-born women in the UK having undergone the procedure. [1]

Sudanese and Eritrean immigrants follow closely, as both countries report 87% and 83% prevalence rates, respectively, contributing substantially to the 53,000 women from the Horn of Africa estimated to have FGM. [1] [3]

Egyptian communities are also prominently affected, with an 87% national rate and over 20,000 women aged 15–49 from high-prevalence Type I and II countries like Egypt residing in England and Wales with FGM. [1]
Other notable communities include those from Sierra Leone (86% prevalence), Ethiopia (65%), and Gambia (76%), where migration patterns have increased the at-risk population. [1]

From 2001 to 2011, the number of women aged 15–49 from FGM-practicing countries in England and Wales rose from 182,000 to 283,000, driven largely by inflows from East and West Africa, including Nigeria and Ethiopia. [3]

Girls born in the UK to mothers from these communities—estimated at 60,000 aged 0–14 in 2011—face heightened risk, particularly during travel to countries of origin, as over three-fifths of mothers giving birth with FGM records hail from high-prevalence Horn of Africa groups. [3]

Prevalence is unevenly distributed, with London boroughs like Southwark (47.4 per 1,000) and Brent (38.9 per 1,000) showing the highest rates due to dense concentrations of these immigrant populations. [3]

While these figures rely on modeled estimates combining migration data and origin-country surveys, they underscore that FGM in the UK is almost exclusively linked to specific immigrant demographics rather than indigenous practices.

The practice of female genital mutilation (FGM) entered the United Kingdom primarily through immigration from African and Middle Eastern countries where it is a traditional cultural rite, with notable increases tied to post-colonial migration patterns starting in the 1960s. [13]

These migratory flows included individuals from nations such as Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia, Somalia, and Nigeria, where prevalence rates exceed 80% in some groups, bringing entrenched customs that persisted within diaspora communities despite the host society's norms. [13]

Early arrivals often formed insular networks in urban areas like London, maintaining practices including FGM on daughters either domestically or via "vacation cutting" abroad, as families sought to preserve ethnic identity amid assimilation pressures.

By the late 1970s and early 1980s, healthcare encounters with FGM complications among immigrant women prompted initial documentation, particularly in hospitals serving African populations, such as those treating Somali refugees who began arriving in larger numbers due to regional instability. [14]

A pivotal response came in 1981 when Efua Dorkenoo, a Ghanaian-born nurse working in the UK, co-founded the Minority Rights Group on Female Excision and Infibulation (later evolving into FORWARD), highlighting the practice's importation via Commonwealth ties and advocating for awareness based on observed cases in immigrant clinics. [14]

This organizational effort underscored how colonial-era connections facilitated small but steady migration from FGM-prevalent regions, with communities like Sudanese and Egyptian expatriates present since the 1950s-1960s, though underreported until medical and activist scrutiny intensified.

The UK's legislative acknowledgment of FGM's presence through immigration culminated in the Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act of 1985, which criminalized the procedure in response to evidence of it occurring within immigrant enclaves and girls being sent overseas for cutting. [13]

Estimates from the period indicated thousands of women living in the UK had undergone FGM prior to arrival, with at-risk UK-born girls in affected families numbering in the hundreds by the mid-1980s, reflecting cumulative effects of decades of selective immigration from high-prevalence areas. [13]

Somali communities, whose significant influx accelerated in the 1980s amid civil war, exemplified this trend, with clinics like Northwick Park Hospital reporting FGM-related treatments among educated refugee women by the late 1980s. [14]
These developments marked the transition from latent cultural carryover to recognized public health and legal concern, driven causally by demographic shifts rather than indigenous adoption.

Initial awareness of female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United Kingdom emerged in the early 1980s amid rising immigration from African countries where the practice is endemic, such as Somalia, Sudan, and parts of West Africa.

Medical professionals in hospitals began encountering cases of young girls presenting with complications from FGM performed either abroad or domestically by traditional "cutters," prompting initial reports in clinical settings and medical discussions.

These encounters highlighted the procedure's health risks, including infections, hemorrhage, and long-term urinary and sexual dysfunction, and raised alarms about its occurrence within British communities.

Parliamentary action followed swiftly, culminating in the Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act 1985, which came into force on 16 September 1985 and criminalized the excision, infibulation, or mutilation of female genitalia in the UK, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment or an unlimited fine.

Introduced as a private member's bill by Conservative MP Marion Roe, the legislation addressed documented instances of FGM being conducted by community practitioners on UK soil, often on girls under 15, and aimed to protect minors from what was described in debates as a harmful cultural import incompatible with British values.
Despite the ban, enforcement proved elusive, with no prosecutions under the Act by the end of the decade, reflecting underreporting and cultural barriers to disclosure. [16]

In the 1990s, reporting remained sporadic and largely confined to healthcare and social services, with isolated media accounts of at-risk children during school holidays—known as "cutting season"—and calls for better safeguarding.

Health authorities issued guidelines for professionals to identify FGM signs, but systemic data collection was absent, and the practice persisted underground due to familial pressures and fears of stigma.

Advocacy by feminists and medical bodies sustained attention, yet official estimates of prevalence were unavailable, and the focus shifted toward education rather than widespread public alarm, as the issue was viewed primarily as affecting specific immigrant enclaves rather than a broader societal threat.

During the early 2000s, documented cases of female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United Kingdom began to emerge more visibly through healthcare records, particularly in maternity services, reflecting heightened awareness following the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 and ongoing immigration from practicing communities.

A 2007 study analyzing official maternity data estimated that 6,256 births in England and Wales in 2001 involved mothers with FGM, rising to 7,109 in 2002, 8,090 in 2003, and 9,032 in 2004—a 44% increase over the four-year period. [19]

These figures, derived from Hospital Episode Statistics coding for FGM-related complications during delivery, indicate growing detections in the National Health Service (NHS), concentrated in urban areas like London (where rates reached 6.3% of relevant maternities in 2004) and other cities such as Birmingham and Manchester.

This uptick in healthcare identifications coincided with broader prevalence estimates suggesting approximately 65,790 women aged 15-49 in England and Wales were living with FGM as of the 2001 census, based on migrant demographics from 29 high-prevalence countries. [19]

For younger females, the same analysis projected over 20,000 girls under 15 at potential risk by the mid-2000s, including those born in the UK to mothers from practicing regions, though direct documentation of procedures on minors remained scarce due to underreporting and lack of routine screening. [19]

Police and criminal justice records, however, showed minimal activity; no successful prosecutions occurred under the 2003 Act during the decade, underscoring that documented cases were predominantly medical rather than forensic, with systemic barriers like cultural stigma and evidentiary challenges limiting formal referrals.

The observed rise likely stemmed from a combination of demographic shifts—increased births among affected communities—and incremental professional training post-legislation, rather than a surge in incidents per se, as prevalence modeling relied on extrapolated country-of-origin rates rather than confirmed UK-performed mutilations. [19]

Specialized NHS clinics for FGM complications, numbering at least ten by 2007, further facilitated identifications, though national data collection remained inconsistent, potentially masking the full extent.

The criminalization of female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United Kingdom began with the Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act 1985, which made it an offense to excise, infibulate, or otherwise mutilate the whole or any part of the labia majora, labia minora, or clitoris of another person, with penalties including up to five years' imprisonment.

This act reflected initial legislative recognition of FGM as a form of child abuse amid growing awareness of cases among immigrant communities, though enforcement was limited due to evidential challenges and cultural sensitivities.

Further refinements came with the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003, which repealed the 1985 legislation and introduced a specific extraterritorial jurisdiction clause, making it illegal for UK nationals or residents to perform, assist, or arrange FGM abroad regardless of the destination country's laws.

The Act defined FGM as altering or mutilating female genitalia for non-medical reasons, with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment for the main offense, and added provisions against aiding, abetting, or counseling FGM.

This evolution was driven by evidence of rising prevalence, including NHS data showing hundreds of FGM-related hospital visits annually, underscoring the need for stronger deterrence against "holiday" cuttings.

The Serious Crime Act 2015 marked a significant escalation by amending the 2003 Act to criminalize failing to protect a girl from FGM risk, with up to seven years' imprisonment for parents or guardians who knowingly allow the procedure, and introducing FGM Protection Orders (FGMPOs) for civil prevention, breach of which carries up to five years.

It also mandated reporting by regulated professionals (e.g., teachers, doctors) of known FGM cases in under-18s to authorities, enhancing proactive intervention amid statistics indicating over 137,000 affected women and girls in the UK by 2016.

These changes reflected causal links between lax prior enforcement—zero convictions from 1985 to 2014—and persistent cultural practices, prioritizing empirical deterrence over multicultural relativism.

Subsequent updates, including the Health and Care Act 2022, expanded mandatory reporting to cover more healthcare settings and improved data collection via the Female Genital Mutilation Enhanced Dataset, facilitating better tracking of cases (e.g., 5,580 newly recorded instances in England from April 2022 to March 2023).

Despite these advancements, critiques from legal analyses highlight ongoing gaps, such as insufficient resources for extraterritorial enforcement and reliance on victim testimony, which has yielded only a handful of convictions post-2015.
The evolution demonstrates a shift from narrow prohibition to comprehensive risk-based criminalization, grounded in verifiable prevalence data rather than unsubstantiated claims of rarity.

In 2019, a woman from east London became the first person convicted under the UK's Female Genital Mutilation Act 1985 for performing FGM on her three-year-old daughter, with the procedure discovered during a medical examination prompted by the child's disclosure at nursery. [21] [22]

The Old Bailey jury found her guilty on February 1, 2019, after evidence showed she had inflicted Type 1 FGM (clitoridectomy) on the girl shortly after birth in 2017, motivated by cultural beliefs from her Somali background. [21]

She was sentenced to 11 years' imprisonment, marking a significant enforcement milestone despite prior failed prosecutions, such as the 2015 acquittal of a doctor accused of FGM during childbirth. [22]

A landmark extraterritorial case in 2023 involved Amina Noor, a British national convicted under section 3 of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 for assisting a non-UK resident in mutilating the genitalia of a three-year-old girl during a trip to Kenya in 2017; she was found guilty at the Central Criminal Court on 26 October 2023 and sentenced to seven years' imprisonment on February 16, 2024, emphasizing the offense's gravity as the first successful prosecution for aiding overseas FGM by a UK citizen. [24] [25]
Her appeal against the sentence was dismissed in July 2024. [24]

In September 2024, Emad Kaky, a 48-year-old former PhD student from Nottingham, was convicted at Leicester Crown Court of conspiring to commit FGM on a young girl, the first such conviction in England and Wales under conspiracy charges linked to the FGM Act. [27] [28]

The plot involved arranging for the procedure abroad, tied to forced marriage intentions within a Kenyan community context; he was initially sentenced to four years in October 2024, but the term was increased to six years and nine months by the Court of Appeal in February 2025 following a referral under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme. [27] [29]
These cases underscore evolving prosecutorial strategies, including conspiracy and extraterritorial applications, amid criticisms of prior leniency in sentencing.
Prosecuting female genital mutilation (FGM) in the UK faces significant evidential challenges, primarily due to the secretive nature of the practice and difficulties in obtaining corroborative proof.

Many cases involve procedures performed abroad on young children, creating jurisdictional hurdles under the extraterritorial provisions of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003, which require establishing a UK nexus such as the victim's or perpetrator's residency.

Physical evidence is often absent or inconclusive by the time authorities investigate, as examinations may occur years later when scarring is ambiguous or healing has progressed, complicating causation links to specific acts. [30]

Victim and witness reluctance constitutes a core barrier, with many survivors, particularly minors, unwilling to testify against family members due to loyalty, fear of reprisal, or cultural stigma framing FGM as a normative rite.
This vulnerability deters reporting, as victims anticipate familial ostracism or community backlash, while the emotional toll of reliving trauma in court further discourages cooperation.
Parliamentary inquiries have noted that such hesitancy undermines case viability, with professionals citing instances where potential witnesses retract statements under pressure. [31]

Institutional factors exacerbate these issues, including inadequate multi-agency coordination between police, health services, and social care, leading to fragmented intelligence and delayed responses.

Up to 2016, no successful convictions occurred despite thousands of identified cases, attributed to insufficient training for frontline officers and prosecutors in handling FGM's cultural context without conflating it with protected traditions, resulting in deprioritization.

Even post-2019's first conviction, low prosecution rates persist, with only a handful of cases reaching court amid resource constraints and inconsistent mandatory reporting by healthcare providers, who often lack confidence in referral pathways. [31] [32]

Cultural persistence within at-risk communities hinders enforcement, as FGM is embedded in traditions from regions like the Horn of Africa, fostering underreporting and resistance to interventions perceived as cultural imperialism.

This dynamic, coupled with broader societal hesitancy to confront community norms aggressively, has led critics to argue that enforcement reflects a reluctance to challenge multiculturalism at the expense of child protection, perpetuating impunity.

In the United Kingdom, education on female genital mutilation (FGM) has been integrated into the national curriculum primarily through compulsory Relationships and Sex Education (RSE) for secondary schools and Relationships Education for primary schools, effective from September 2020. [34]

Secondary schools are required to teach about FGM as part of RSE, alongside other harmful practices, to raise awareness of risks, safeguarding, and legal protections under the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003. [35]

This statutory framework aims to equip pupils with knowledge to recognize FGM, understand its illegality, and report concerns, often delivered via Personal, Social, Health and Economic (PSHE) education modules.

For primary schools, while FGM education is not explicitly mandated in Relationships Education, guidance and resources encourage age-appropriate integration, particularly for Year 5 and 6 pupils, focusing on body safety, consent, and harmful cultural practices. [37]

The Department for Education has endorsed lesson plans, such as those from the PSHE Association and National FGM Centre, which include interactive activities on identifying FGM risks during holidays or within communities. [38]
These resources emphasize safeguarding, with teachers trained to identify at-risk pupils from communities where FGM prevalence is higher, such as those of Somali, Egyptian, or Sudanese origin.

Teacher training forms a critical component of curriculum integration, with programs like those from the National FGM Centre providing workshops on FGM recognition, legal duties, and pupil engagement. [40]

Government-backed resource packs, including case studies and awareness materials, support schools in embedding FGM prevention into broader child protection efforts, though implementation varies by local authority. [41]
Campaigners have advocated for earlier primary inclusion, arguing that delayed awareness misses opportunities to prevent cases during school holidays. [42]
Despite these efforts, evaluations indicate that consistent delivery depends on school resources and staff confidence, with ongoing calls for mandatory primary-level content.

In the United Kingdom, healthcare professionals are subject to mandatory reporting requirements for female genital mutilation (FGM) under the Serious Crime Act 2015, which mandates regulated health and social care professionals, including doctors, nurses, and midwives, to report known cases of FGM in girls under 18 to the police within one month of becoming aware of it.

This duty applies when the professional directly observes physical signs of FGM or is informed by the girl herself that it has been carried out, aiming to facilitate early intervention and protection.
Failure to report without reasonable grounds can result in professional sanctions, though criminal penalties are not imposed; the focus is on safeguarding rather than punishment.

The National Health Service (NHS) integrates FGM safeguarding into its broader child protection frameworks, with guidelines requiring all clinical staff to undergo training on recognizing FGM risks, particularly in high-prevalence communities such as those from Somalia, Sudan, and Egypt.

NHS England reports that between April 2015 and March 2023, over 25,000 FGM cases were recorded in healthcare datasets, with safeguarding referrals triggered in cases involving minors or at-risk individuals.

Healthcare providers must conduct risk assessments during antenatal care, routine examinations, and consultations with girls from affected diasporas, documenting any concerns in electronic records shared across services to enable multi-agency responses.

Mandatory reporting intersects with Female Genital Mutilation Protection Orders (FGMPOs), where healthcare evidence often supports applications to courts for interim protections, such as restricting travel or requiring medical examinations.

A 2021 Home Office evaluation found that healthcare-initiated reports contributed to 15% of FGMPO applications, though implementation challenges include under-detection due to cultural stigma and inconsistent training, with only 60% of maternity units reporting full staff compliance in audits.

Critics, including reports from the British Medical Association, argue that the system's reliance on voluntary disclosure limits efficacy, as many cases remain unreported until complications arise, such as during childbirth where Type III FGM (infibulation) necessitates surgical deinfibulation.

Despite these measures, data from the Health and Social Care Information Centre indicate persistent gaps, with fewer than 1,000 mandatory reports to police annually despite higher healthcare identifications, attributed to fears of family repercussions and resource constraints in primary care.

Multi-agency safeguarding hubs, mandated by local authorities, coordinate healthcare inputs with social services, but a 2019 NSPCC analysis highlighted that only 40% of identified at-risk girls receive proactive follow-up, underscoring the need for enhanced inter-professional protocols.

Female Genital Mutilation Protection Orders (FGMPOs) were introduced in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland under the Serious Crime Act 2015, effective from July 2015, as a civil measure to safeguard girls and women at risk of or subjected to FGM. [43]

These orders, issued by the Family Court, impose tailored conditions such as prohibiting the removal of a protected person from the UK, requiring disclosure of passport details or travel plans, mandating attendance at medical examinations, or restricting contact with family members who may perpetrate FGM. [43]

Applications can be made by the individual at risk, relevant third parties designated by the Lord Chancellor (such as local authorities or police), or others with court permission, including children via a legal representative. [43]

Breaching an FGMPO constitutes a criminal offense punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, or contempt of court with up to two years' detention, and can trigger arrest warrants or police prosecution.
Usage of FGMPOs has remained limited relative to estimated risks, with only 18 orders issued in the first five months following their launch in 2015. [44]
Annual data from the Ministry of Justice tracks new cases, but overall numbers indicate sporadic application, often in conjunction with broader safeguarding proceedings. [45]
Orders can be interim, time-limited, or indefinite, and may be varied or discharged upon application, allowing flexibility in response to changing family dynamics or resolved risks.
Family interventions complement FGMPOs through social services and multi-agency safeguarding protocols, focusing on early risk identification and preventive engagement.

Local authorities conduct risk assessments using frameworks that evaluate factors like family history of FGM, planned travel to high-prevalence countries, or reluctance for intimate medical exams, often triggered by referrals from healthcare providers or schools. [46]

Social workers engage families directly, discussing legal prohibitions and health consequences to dissuade perpetration, while exploring influences from extended relatives or community pressures; in cases of confirmed risk to siblings or cousins, interventions extend to wider kin networks.

Where voluntary compliance fails, interventions escalate to coercive measures, including applications for Emergency Protection Orders under the Children Act 1989 to temporarily remove a child to safety or restrict parental actions. [46]

Supportive elements, such as referrals to counseling via NHS FGM clinics or community groups, address psychological impacts on at-risk or affected individuals, though emphasis remains on disrupting family intent rather than post-harm remediation. [46]
Mandatory reporting duties require professionals to notify police of observed FGM in under-18s, integrating family interventions with criminal investigations.

Female genital mutilation (FGM) causes immediate physical complications such as severe pain, haemorrhage, genital swelling, infections (including tetanus), urinary retention, and wound disruption, which can result in shock or death, particularly when performed without anaesthesia or sterile instruments. [47] [7]
These risks apply across WHO-classified types of FGM, from partial clitoral removal (Type 1) to infibulation (Type 3), with higher severity correlating to greater immediate harm.

Long-term physical effects include chronic urinary tract infections, painful urination, menstrual difficulties due to obstructed flow, vaginal infections, sexual pain and reduced satisfaction, keloid scarring, and reproductive issues like infertility or cysts. [47] [7]

Obstetric complications are prominent, encompassing prolonged labour, excessive postpartum bleeding, higher caesarean rates, and elevated newborn mortality; women with Type 3 FGM often require deinfibulation surgeries for safe delivery. [47]

In the United Kingdom, National Health Service (NHS) records document affected women presenting with these sequelae, including recurrent infections and childbirth emergencies, prompting specialized gynaecological interventions and antenatal screening protocols.

Psychological impacts manifest as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety disorders, depression, and diminished self-esteem, often stemming from the non-consensual trauma and lifelong bodily alterations. [47]

Systematic reviews confirm associations between FGM and adverse mental health outcomes, including panic disorders, somatization, and emotional suppression, with 14 of 16 studies reporting at least one such link. [48]

UK-based survivors frequently report flashbacks, nightmares, sleep disturbances, and self-harm, exacerbating isolation and complicating mental health access within communities where FGM persists culturally.

The National Health Service (NHS) in England and Wales faces substantial long-term healthcare expenditures attributable to female genital mutilation (FGM), estimated at £100 million annually based on 2015/16 data, encompassing treatment for complications among an estimated 137,000 affected women and girls. [49]

This figure, derived from hospital episode statistics, unit costs from NHS reference data, and prevalence estimates, includes a sensitivity range of £33 million to £184 million to account for data uncertainties and underreporting; psychological care alone accounts for £66 million, covering excess cases of depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder treated via primary, secondary, and mental health services. [49]

Long-term physical complications contribute £33 million yearly, primarily through recurrent urinary tract infections, dyspareunia management, and elevated obstetric interventions such as caesarean sections (£4 million for 1,036 excess cases at £3,941 each) and instrumental deliveries (£3 million for 1,056 cases).

These healthcare demands impose a persistent fiscal strain on public resources, as FGM-related conditions often require lifelong management, including de-infibulation procedures (£343,000 annually) and unquantified issues like cysts, infertility, and heightened HIV transmission risks due to insufficient UK-specific evidence. [49]

Obstetric costs are amplified by FGM's association with prolonged labor, hemorrhage, and tears, necessitating specialized maternity care that exceeds standard deliveries and contributes to broader NHS pressures in specialties like gynaecology and urology. [49]

The predominance of psychological and chronic physical burdens underscores a societal cost beyond acute interventions, with potential underestimation from unmet needs, as enhanced FGM datasets from 2015 onward reveal only partial attendance patterns.

Societally, these expenditures reflect opportunity costs for the UK economy, diverting funds from other priorities amid rising prevalence linked to migration from high-risk regions, though direct productivity losses—such as reduced workforce participation from chronic pain or mental health sequelae—remain unquantified in national studies. [49]

Intergenerational persistence exacerbates long-term liabilities, as untreated complications in mothers correlate with adverse birth outcomes, perpetuating cycles of healthcare dependency and straining social services for affected families.

Government reports highlight ongoing demands for reconstructive surgeries to mitigate pain and dysfunction, yet policy gaps in funding limit scalability, implying escalating costs without effective cultural interventions.
NHS England data from the Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) Enhanced Dataset indicate a rise in recorded healthcare attendances related to FGM.

For the financial year April 2023 to March 2024, there were 14,355 such attendances across NHS trusts and general practices in England, involving 6,655 individual women and girls where FGM was identified. [10]
This marked an approximately 15% increase from 12,475 attendances in 2022-2023. [10]
These statistics reflect only cases encountered in healthcare settings and added to the dataset, capturing a fraction of total prevalence due to underdiagnosis, stigma, and non-presentation for care.
Cumulative records since the dataset's inception in April 2015 total 37,615 individuals with FGM noted in England. [10]

No national population-based prevalence surveys have been conducted or updated in the 2020s, leaving reliance on healthcare proxies and extrapolations from migration patterns from FGM-practicing countries.

Earlier modeling estimated around 137,000 women and girls born in FGM-practicing countries residing in England and Wales, with approximately 103,000 aged 15–49 estimated to have undergone FGM (as of 2011 data), a figure likely conservative given subsequent immigration and the absence of eradication evidence.

The uptick in identifications may stem from improved clinician awareness and mandatory reporting protocols rather than solely incidence changes, though experts attribute part of it to ongoing risks in affected communities. [50]

Quarterly data for January to March 2024 showed continued activity, with ongoing additions to the dataset underscoring persistent exposure among at-risk groups, particularly those under 18 newly recorded.

Despite enhancements to FGM legislation, prosecutions remain infrequent, with official data indicating only a handful of convictions since 2015 amid thousands of identified FGM cases in England and Wales annually via NHS datasets. [2]

Notable recent cases include the October 2023 conviction of Amina Noor, a British citizen of Somali origin, for child cruelty by wilful neglect and perverting the course of justice in relation to arranging the genital mutilation of a three-year-old British girl during a 2006 trip to Kenya; Noor was sentenced in February 2024. [52]

In September 2024, Emad Kaky became the first person convicted in England and Wales of conspiring to commit FGM, after arranging for a girl to undergo the procedure in Iraq in 2019 alongside a forced marriage; initially sentenced to four and a half years' imprisonment, his term was increased to seven years by the Court of Appeal in January 2025 following referral under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme. [29]

Ongoing enforcement efforts by the Crown Prosecution Service emphasize evidence thresholds for rare cultural practices, requiring corroboration beyond victim testimony due to potential family pressures, yet critics from child protection advocates highlight persistent under-prosecution linked to evidentiary challenges and community reluctance to report. [2]

The Home Office continues to support multi-agency protocols, including risk assessments during school holidays ("cutting season"), but as of 2024, conviction rates lag behind prevalence estimates, underscoring gaps in implementation despite legal strengthening.

Female genital mutilation (FGM) in the United States refers to procedures that intentionally alter or injure the female genital organs for non-medical reasons, including partial or total removal of the external genitalia, a practice prohibited by federal statute since 1996 and occurring chiefly among certain immigrant groups from high-prevalence regions in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. [1] [2]

The federal law, codified at 18 U.S.C. § 116, criminalizes performing, assisting, or facilitating FGM, with penalties up to five years imprisonment, and explicitly rejects religious, cultural, or traditional justifications as defenses. [1]

While the procedure offers no health benefits and inflicts immediate and long-term physical and psychological harm, including pain, infection, urinary issues, sexual dysfunction, and increased childbirth complications, enforcement remains challenging due to underreporting, victim reluctance, and cultural secrecy. [2]

Estimates from U.S. government analyses indicate that over 500,000 women and girls in the United States have either undergone FGM abroad or face risk of undergoing it domestically or during travel, derived from demographic data on immigrants and their descendants from countries with FGM rates exceeding 20 percent. [4]

This figure underscores a persistent public health and human rights issue, concentrated in urban areas with large diasporas from nations like Somalia, Egypt, and Nigeria, where prevalence can approach 90 percent in origin populations. [5]

Federal agencies, including the Department of Justice and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have pursued prosecutions in notable cases involving practitioners and transporters of minors, though convictions are infrequent owing to evidentiary hurdles and judicial scrutiny of the law's scope. [6]

State-level responses vary, with some enacting specific bans reinforcing federal prohibitions and others relying on general child abuse or assault statutes, reflecting uneven legislative attention to the problem. [8]

Ongoing federal initiatives, such as the STOP FGM Act of 2019, mandate interagency coordination for prevention, education, and reporting, aiming to address data gaps and community outreach amid criticisms of inadequate surveillance and cultural sensitivity debates that sometimes impede intervention. [9]

A 2016 analysis by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), drawing on data from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and Demographic and Health Surveys, estimated that 513,000 women and girls in the United States were either affected by female genital mutilation (FGM) or at risk of undergoing it. [5]

This figure represented a tripling of prior estimates from 1990, largely attributable to increased immigration from countries where FGM prevalence exceeds 50 percent, such as Somalia, Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia. [11]
The at-risk population primarily consists of girls under 18 from immigrant families, with the highest concentrations in communities originating from sub-Saharan Africa and parts of the Middle East.

Without routine tracking or mandatory reporting in all states, actual prevalence likely exceeds documented figures, as procedures often occur covertly to evade legal scrutiny.

Underreporting is exacerbated by clandestine practices, including "cutting parties" organized within immigrant enclaves in urban areas like Minneapolis, Seattle, and New York, where girls are subjected to FGM by traditional practitioners or family members. [14]

Medicalized procedures, performed by health workers in clinics or hospitals to mimic legitimacy, further obscure detection, with some surveys indicating support for such approaches among affected communities to reduce perceived harms while preserving cultural norms. [15]
These factors contribute to hidden caseloads, as victims rarely seek care due to stigma, fear of reprisal, or distrust of authorities, limiting empirical verification.

The primary victims of female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in the United States are girls under 18 years old from first- or second-generation immigrant families originating from countries with high FGM/C prevalence rates, where the practice involves non-consensual procedures on minors typically aligned with World Health Organization classifications of Types I (clitoridectomy), II (excision), or III (infibulation). [16]

In 2012, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates indicated that 513,000 women and girls were at risk, with 169,000 (about one-third) being girls under 18, reflecting a 314% increase in the minor at-risk population since 1990 due to immigration-driven demographic shifts rather than rising origin-country rates. [16]

These at-risk groups are overwhelmingly from African nations, comprising 97% of the total, with the largest shares from Egypt (20%), Ethiopia (18%), and Somalia (12%), where national FGM/C rates exceed 70-90% among females. [5] [16]

Second-generation U.S.-born daughters form a substantial portion of the younger at-risk cohort, as parents may perpetuate origin-country customs despite acculturation pressures, though empirical data show no reliable measurement of actual U.S.-performed incidences due to underreporting and clandestine nature. [5]

Risk is amplified by "cutting vacations," where families transport prepubescent girls abroad for the procedure to evade U.S. scrutiny, or through domestic underground practitioners, linking causal persistence directly to familial ties with high-prevalence diasporas.

Claims minimizing FGM/C as voluntary cultural choice lack empirical support, as procedures target non-consenting minors—often infants or young girls—causing immediate risks like hemorrhage and infection alongside long-term complications such as urinary issues, sexual dysfunction, and psychological trauma, corroborated by clinical outcomes in affected communities. [2] [16]

Hospital data from immigrant-heavy regions reveal elevated presentations for FGM/C-related complications, underscoring non-voluntary imposition without evidence of affirmative minor consent in documented cases.

Estimates indicate that female genital mutilation (FGM) risks and occurrences in the United States are disproportionately concentrated in metropolitan areas and states with substantial immigrant populations from countries where the practice is culturally entrenched, such as Somalia, Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan.

A 2013 analysis using U.S. Census data identified the highest numbers of women and girls at risk in the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area (65,893), followed by Washington-Arlington-Alexandria (51,411) and Minneapolis-St. Paul-Bloomington (37,417), with these five largest metros accounting for about 40% of the national total of approximately 507,000 at risk. These patterns reflect immigration-driven demographics, as foreign-born individuals from the 27 WHO-designated FGM-prevalent countries comprise over 90% of those estimated at risk.

In Minnesota, home to one of the largest Somali diaspora communities in the U.S.—with over 80,000 Somalis resettled since the 1990s—FGM risks are elevated due to the practice's near-universal prevalence (98%) in Somalia.

State health data highlight ongoing concerns in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area, where underground networks persist despite awareness campaigns, and an estimated 44,000 women and girls are at risk statewide. [17] [5]

In Michigan, the 2017 federal prosecution of a Detroit-area doctor for performing FGM on at least seven girls aged 6 to 8—primarily from the Dawoodi Bohra Muslim sect, which maintains the practice despite origins outside traditional African contexts—underscored localized underground operations in immigrant enclaves.

State-level variations align with immigration gateways: California (57,000 at risk), New York (48,000), and Minnesota lead, comprising over half of national figures alongside Maryland, New Jersey, Texas, Virginia, and Washington. [5]

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) tracking, derived from census and health surveys, notes under-detection in rural areas and non-gateway states due to clandestine practices, limited reporting, and cultural stigma, potentially understating true incidence beyond urban clusters. [2]

Sporadic reports of female genital mutilation (FGM) among small immigrant communities from African countries appeared in the United States during the 1970s and 1980s, coinciding with initial waves of refugees from nations such as Ethiopia and Somalia where the practice is culturally entrenched. Medical documentation first emerged in refugee health clinics, where providers identified complications like infections and urinary issues in affected women, marking an initial shift from general ignorance of the procedure's presence domestically to empirical recognition of its physical harms.
By the early 1990s, awareness intensified through refugee resettlement data compiled by health agencies, revealing patterns of FGM-related health risks among arrivals from high-prevalence regions.
This documentation prompted heightened scrutiny, culminating in congressional proposals to address the issue.

A companion bill, H.R. 941, followed in 1995 under Representative Barbara-Rose Collins, further elevating the practice in policy discussions prior to enactment.

The World Health Organization's 1996 classification of FGM into four types—emphasizing its non-therapeutic nature and severe consequences—reinforced U.S. discourse by providing a standardized framework for viewing the procedure as medically harmful rather than culturally neutral. [25]

This international benchmark, combined with domestic refugee health findings, facilitated a transition from anecdotal clinic reports to structured recognition of FGM's causality in chronic pain, obstetric complications, and psychological trauma among affected populations.

Empirical data from immigrant cohorts show that geographic isolation and community cohesion maintain prevalence levels akin to homelands, rather than inevitable assimilation-driven decline.

The Federal Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act of 1996 established the first nationwide ban on FGM, criminalizing the knowing performance, attempt, or conspiracy to perform any clitoridectomy, excision, or infibulation on the labia majora, labia minora, or clitoris of a female under 18 years of age, classifying it as a felony punishable by fines and up to five years imprisonment. [24] [1]

Codified at 18 U.S.C. § 116, the statute included a narrow affirmative defense for procedures deemed medically necessary to the person's health and performed by a licensed medical professional in that jurisdiction, but no allowances for cultural, religious, or customary practices. [1]
This legislation framed FGM as a form of child abuse under federal criminal law, targeting acts regardless of parental consent or perpetrator intent beyond knowledge of the procedure.

In 2013, Congress enacted the Transport for Female Genital Mutilation Act as an amendment, extending prohibitions to include knowingly transporting or attempting to transport any person across a U.S. state line or international border with intent to subject them to FGM, thereby addressing "vacation cutting" practices where minors are taken abroad for the procedure. [30]
This expansion reinforced federal jurisdiction over interstate and foreign elements, maintaining the focus on protecting minors without cultural exemptions.

The Strengthening the Opposition to Female Genital Mutilation Act of 2020 (STOP FGM Act), signed into law on January 5, 2021, further amended 18 U.S.C. § 116 to increase the maximum penalty to 10 years imprisonment, explicitly affirm prosecution viability through links to interstate or foreign commerce, and clarify that the offense applies irrespective of the victim's consent or the perpetrator's beliefs about cultural or religious requirements. [9] [31]

These enhancements marked a shift toward stricter enforcement mechanisms and zero-tolerance policy, emphasizing FGM's classification as non-consensual child harm without health-based justifications beyond the existing medical exception. [32]
The federal prohibition remains limited to acts on minors under 18, with no direct criminalization of procedures on consenting adults, though transportation offenses apply more broadly.
As of 2025, more than 40 states have enacted explicit statutes criminalizing female genital mutilation (FGM), often as standalone offenses or integrated into child abuse and endangerment laws. [33]
Early legislation emerged in the mid-1990s, with Texas passing the first state ban in 1995, followed by New York in 1996. [34]
These laws typically prohibit the knowing performance of FGM on minors, with some extending protections to adults.
State laws exhibit significant variations in scope and penalties.

For instance, Minnesota's statute includes a "vacation cutting" provision that criminalizes transporting a minor out of state or abroad for FGM, addressing circumvention via international travel. [33]

Penalties range from misdemeanors for lesser procedures to felonies carrying sentences of up to life imprisonment in cases involving severe harm, death, or repeat offenses, as seen in statutes like California's, which escalates based on injury extent. [33]
Several states hold parents or guardians liable alongside performers, enhancing deterrence.

Approximately nine states lack dedicated FGM prohibitions, depending instead on general assault, battery, or child maltreatment statutes, which may not adequately address the procedure's non-therapeutic nature or cultural drivers. [34]

Equality Now's assessments highlight these gaps as weakening enforcement, as generic laws often fail to signal zero tolerance for FGM specifically, potentially allowing persistence through prosecutorial reluctance or evidentiary challenges in culturally insular communities. [33]
Comprehensive bans correlate with higher reporting incentives and specialized training for officials, underscoring the need for uniform specificity to close loopholes.

The United States has not ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) or the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), despite signing CEDAW in 1980, limiting direct binding obligations under these instruments that condemn female genital mutilation (FGM) via general recommendations such as CEDAW General Recommendation No. 14 and CRC General Comment No. 14.
